utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you would all have received the decision of the Appeals Chamber in this case. Consequent on that decision which is dated the 16th, the proceedings in this case are adjourned for a minimum of three months and the state of health of the accused will be reassessed before determining when the trial should commence. The UNDU doctor will report weekly on the health of the accused. The gastroenterologist is to examine the accused once every month or more frequently, if required, and submit a report thereon. Dr. de Man, the Court-appointed psychiatrist is to examine the accused once every three weeks and submit a report after each examination. The Chamber received a motion for provisional release from the Defence of the accused Stanisic. There is a reference in that report to a report from the treating psychiatrist, Dr. Petrovic, and reliance is placed on that report. The Chamber will require that that report be submitted to it and to the other parties in the proceedings. It is, of course, necessary that the application for provisional release be dealt with as quickly as possible and in that regard, Mr. Groome, I would expect that the Prosecution would be in a position to provide its response tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, the Chamber would then be in a position to give its decision on Friday. There is one matter, Mr. Knoops, that is raised by your application. It is clear that the Appeals Chamber had in mind a regime of continued and regular examination of the health of the accused. Were provisional release to be granted, would there not be logistical problems in ensuring that the Chamber is provided with reliable reports? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, we are mindful of the concerns of the Chamber in terms of compliance with the potential provisional release conditions. Yet, also in light of the report of Dr. Falke of today indicating already the report of Dr. Petrovic opining that she has reached a plateau in her ability to treat Mr. Stanisic without assistance of a multi-disciplinary team in a medical environment, we believe that could outweigh any practicalities or logistical obstacles which might arise from this application. In the second place, we believe that in case Your Honours would grant such a release for medical treatment in a non-custodial environment, the Chamber has authority to, for instance, order the treating doctors to report directly to either Dr. Falke and the registry or directly to the Chamber while, for instance, Dr. Petrovic is, of course, at liberty to visit on a regular basis that facility where Mr. Stanisic, by then, would hopefully reside. If the Chamber would have any doubt as to the credibility of such reports, we also believe that, for instance, on a regular basis, Dr. de Man could visit that facility where Mr. Stanisic, by then, would reside in order to provide the Chamber with the most objective reports as possible. However, in light of the history of this case, Your Honour, I believe with all due respect that the reports which have been filed until so far by the treating doctors from Belgrade do not lack any form of credibility or subjectiveness, but I understand Your Honours' concern that also in light of the importance of this matter, that indeed some form of supervision could be administered in order to ensure that the Chamber will receive, and the course the other parties, the most optimal objective information. So we don't believe that the argument which is concern of the Chamber could hamper the basis and the foundation of our request. As Your Honours may have noticed, the Defence was informed last Friday by the medical staff themselves, which is a clear indication that the medical staff considers the situation as extreme grave of Mr. Stanisic, also evidenced by the attack Sunday night. I was informed that Dr. Falke returned during the night to the detention centre to conduct medical care, and I have to say that we were, ourselves, also witness of some of those events. In this regard, Your Honour, the motion mentions that several guarantees could be provided to the Court, if necessary, in case the Court would think that the existing guarantees would not fully comply with the new motion for provisional release. In this regard, we were informed that both governments of Montenegro and of Serbia will do their utmost best to provide, maybe this week, the required additional guarantees in order to facilitate the potential transfer of the accused to any of the medical institutions in those countries, and in light of the concerns also raised by other doctors in this case, we believe that also those countries will do their best to comply with any of the provisions and conditions the Court might set. But as to your concrete request and question as to the reporting system, I don't see a problem in the continuation the Court has in mind on a weekly or three-weekly basis by both the physicians who are treating the accused by then and the doctors from The Hague who could go to that specific facility. I hope this may clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me say at the outset that I think it's inappropriate for Mr. Stanisic to be placed on provisional release at this time. I have prepared some submissions in that regard and in light of the Chamber's urgent time schedule, if I could make them, but I've also -- have planned to make some observations just about how in this three months, the Prosecution believes steps should be taken to ensure not only that Mr. Stanisic is in optimal health for the continuation of the trial but also that the Chamber has before it all of the information that it needs to make its assessment at the end of that period. And some of that information is also relevant to the provisional release, so if I can indulge the Court and have a bit of time to explain all of our submissions, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think the -- are there steps that the -- that can be taken to ensure that the greatest probability that we will resume in September or August and we will be at that time able to proceed expeditiously. With respect to Mr. Stanisic's health, I believe that there are. I think we must consider that everything that can be done to ensure Mr. Stanisic is in optimal physical health at the end of this three-month period is done, lest we find ourselves in the very same position that we are in today, and I think we must carefully consider that everything that can be done to ensure Mr. Stanisic is in optimal mental health at the end of the three-month period and that the Chamber has a current assessment of his psychiatric situation available. With respect to his physical health, the current regime of daily medical reports gives the Chamber the information it needs from Dr. Falke, the primary care physician of Mr. Stanisic. I submit that it's critical that the Chamber and the parties continue to receive these reports at least on a weekly basis so that his progress toward optimal health can be monitored. Looking back at Judge Parker's investigation into Mr. Milosevic's death, it became clear that there was shortcomings in the UNDU's regime of administering medications to detainees. The Chamber must satisfy itself that Mr. Stanisic is getting all of the medicine that he requires when he should be getting that medicine during this time period to ensure that he reaches optimal health. I note in this latest report that he's now on a regime of suppositories. We don't know whether he's administering those himself or whether a nurse or medical staff is administering those. It would seem it if he's administering those himself, there is the possibility that these could simply be flushed down the toilet rather than being actually used. I believe this requires the Chamber to make an inquiry with the UN detention unit and also requires the Chamber to periodically order blood tests to establish whether the appropriate medicines are present in the appropriate levels and that other non-prescribed substances are not present. Also, learning from the experience of Mr. Milosevic's death as investigated by Judge Parker, it was clear that Mr. Milosevic's diet may also have played a part. During his detention he consumed large amounts of grapefruit, according to a diet he was on, and that compromised or possibly compromised the medications he received. In this case given Mr. Stanisic's intestinal complication, it seems prudent to have some inquiry made of his diet, perhaps as simple as having the gastroenterologist review his diet and make suggestions, if necessary. I note that last Friday, we did receive the first gastroenterology report of Dr. Cazemir. I think it is imperative that the Chamber and the parties continue to receive these reports. I note that it appears that Dr. Cazemir conducts one in-person examination per month and then does consultations with Mr. Stanisic over the phone each week. Given Mr. Stanisic's recent exacerbation of pouchitis, the Chamber may take the view that more frequent visits are required, and certainly in light of the information as it's being characterised today, it seems to fly in the face of the seriousness that's being attributed to his condition presently if Dr. Cazemir still feels comfortable in conducting weekly assessments of Mr. Stanisic's condition over the telephone and not personally examining him. Ensuring he is in optimal psychiatric health. Recent reports have been encouraging in that Mr. Stanisic has seen measurable although modest improvements in his depression. While this has been the source of the most significant impediments for progress in this trial, it is unfortunately the area in which the Chamber receives the least direct information from his treating psychiatrist, Dr. Petrovic. She has never filed a report with the Chamber. And the Chamber has only hearsay evidence about her treatment schedule and her treatment plan. The Prosecution submits that this must change. From the information that I have been able to glean from the testimony of Dr. de Man and Dr. Falke, it appears that Dr. Petrovic travels back and forth from Serbia. It seems that in times an entire week or more can intervene between his therapeutic sessions with Dr. Petrovic. The question that must be asked is whether such intervals between treatments are appropriate given his present mental state and whether more frequent sessions would yield a quicker, more certain improvement in his mental health. The Chamber and the parties should also be regularly informed about the medications Mr. Stanisic is taking. I note that Dr. Cazemir in his report dated the 14th of May 2008, states that Mr. Stanisic is currently on mirtazapine. If you recall on the 7th of April, 2008, Dr. de Man testified that in the beginning of March, Mr. Stanisic was placed on mirtazapine, a drug whose known side effects include night-time hallucinations. Dr. de Man, in light of Mr. Stanisic's report of night-time hallucinations, recommended taking Mr. Stanisic off mirtazapine and placed on an older form of anti-depressants known as tricyclics. Dr. de Man stated that Dr. Petrovic concurred with his view and Mr. Stanisic's medications had been switched. Now, whether Dr. Cazemir looked at an older list of medications or whether there has been an oversight and his medication has not been changed and he's still receiving mirtazapine, it seems that this is a matter that the Chamber must be in a position to raise with the UN detention unit. At the conclusion of this three-month period the Chamber must reassess the health of the accused. Mr. Stanisic is presently fit to stand trial and the Appeals Chamber has not contradicted the Chamber on this point. However, the Appeals Chamber does recognise, as this Chamber has always recognised and as the Prosecution has always recognised, that Mr. Stanisic's mental health is an inexorable component of his overall health and as such we must always be mindful of it. The Prosecution will be proposing in a written submission hopefully filed later today or tomorrow and in that we go into detail in -- in what I'm about to talk about with respect to his psychiatric health. But I would submit to the Chamber as directed by the Appeals Chamber, the Chamber will have to reassess Mr. Stanisic's health at the end of the three-month period and as such will have to consider his psychiatric health in an overall assessment. With this in mind, I make the following submission: Last Friday, my staff and I had an informal meeting with staff from the Pieter Baan Centre in Utrecht, the well-respected institute of forensic psychiatry here in the Netherlands. In this informal meeting we met with Eric Hejderberg, the director of the institute, and Ms. Marsha de Boer, one of the senior lawyers responsible for administration of the programme. It is part of the NIFP, which is the Dutch government's department which is responsible for assessing the mental health of subjects of the Dutch criminal justice system and is also responsible for meeting the mental health needs of detainees in Dutch facilities. The Pieter Baan Centre is a secure detention facility with the capacity to do comprehensive psychiatric evaluations. They do over 8.000 evaluations per year with roughly 225 of them being done on an in-house basis. Some of these evaluations are related to the psychiatric state at the time a crime is committed. Others are fitness to stand trial, and finally, what I will be suggesting is very appropriate in the circumstances we know find ourselves in, finally, they investigate the appropriateness of detention for detained persons. That is one the central tasks that they are assigned to do, whether or not someone is fit still to be detained or whether they should be -- some alternative arrangement should be made. These evaluations are conducted by a multi-disciplinary team of psychiatrists, psychologists, and licensed social workers who do comprehensive testing and observations of a subject and issue a detailed report of their findings. They have a roster of over 600 mental health professionals who they call on to do these evaluations depending on the particular requirements of a situation. Mr. Dr. de Man is one of these associated psychiatrists. They regularly work with subjects from different countries and are confident in their ability to assess someone from Serbia. They in fact have a Serbian social worker on their staff capable of participating in any evaluation of Mr. Stanisic. They have the capacity to make all the necessary arrangements for necessary interpreters. An integral part of their evaluation is an investigation into the likelihood that a subject a seeking some advantage by manipulating symptoms and complaints regarding their mental health. In light of some of the evidence that is before the Chamber, there would be a benefit in having this professionally explored. It is the Prosecution's view that it would be prudent to order an evaluation of Mr. Stanisic during this three-month period. Hopefully near the end of the period, so that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, when you said "in light of some of the evidence that is before the Chamber," are you suggesting that the Chamber has had evidence of manipulation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the fitness hearing, there were two pieces of evidence that I think would be consistent with someone who is attempting to manipulate the system. The first was that testimony -- or Mr. Stanisic's own report to Dr. Mimica that on a single day he went to two different psychiatrists, made similar complaints, received prescriptions for two different sets of drugs and then declined to take any of the drugs, and then secondly, the report by the Serbian government on Mr. Stanisic's whereabouts on a particular day, a day when he was claiming to be, as one Defence expert characterised it, essentially an invalid where he spent over an 11-hour day visiting a number of locations around the city. So I believe that there is some cause for concern. I believe it is a matter that should be explored and it is a matter that is regularly explored as part of an evaluation by the Pieter Baan Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I must say that I myself don't see that as necessarily indicating manipulation, but please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is the Prosecution's view that it would be prudent to order an evaluation of Mr. Stanisic during this three-month period so that near the end of the period, the Chamber would have a reliable, comprehensive and current assessment of his mental health. There is a waiting list to get into the Peter Bahn Centre and although Dr. Hejderberg and Mrs. De Boer could not specify the length of the period, they were optimistic that if the process were commenced in the coming weeks they would be able to complete an evaluation of Mr. Stanisic within the three-month period. Their recommendation was that prior to Mr. Stanisic being formally evaluated by them, that they engage in a process with the Chamber with input from the parties to precisely articulate the questions that would be most helpful to the Chamber, thereby allowing them to customise the examination in a way that yields the most useful information for the Chamber. I was clear with them during this meeting that the Prosecution was simply trying to inform itself of the possibilities available and would convey the information to the Chamber. I advised them that should the Chamber wish to explore the matter further, the Chamber and the registrar would be in further contact. It is their view that they would be able to assist the Chamber by conducting a thorough evaluation of Mr. Stanisic and provide not only a written report but would be willing to come to court to discuss their findings. It is my position that such an evaluation would be very useful to the Chamber and would give the Chamber great confidence in whatever determination it makes at the end of the three-month period. Your Honour, they also provided us with books on what they do and a brochure of what they document. I have two copies. I'm willing to provide them to the Chamber and Defence counsel if the Chamber is interested in receiving them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please pass them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As I noted, Your Honour, the primary basis for the provisional release application appears to me to be that it's detention is no long appropriate for Mr. Stanisic. Given the seriousness of this question and the seriousness of the charges, this is one of the areas that they regularly, the Pieter Baan Centre regularly advises the Dutch courts on is whether or not detention is appropriate for particular subjects and it seems to me that the more prudent course of action would be seeking their professional evaluation on this rather than some of the information that -- which is presently before the Chamber which I'd like to address now. With respect to provisional release, first as the Chamber heard in the fitness hearings, Mr. Stanisic's depression was in significant part a reaction to recent detention. You heard Dr. Mimica describe it as a reactive depression which would dissipate over time. Dr. Mimica's prognosis has proved true and we are -- up until this filing today, this report today, we have been seeing a modest but measurable abatement of his depression. We can only fully expect that should Mr. Stanisic be placed on provisional release that he will relapse with the same complaints when he returns to detention. He is getting proper care here as evidenced by his improvement. His care is now being closely supervised by the Court and all of the recent optimistic assessments of his future well being have been predicated on the assumption that his detention would continue. Living in a detention facility and receiving this complete set of medical services he is currently receiving, he has shown improvement. Secondly, if the Chamber agrees that the evaluation of the Pieter Baan Centre would assist in its consideration of future hearings in September, then his release or return to Belgrade would make that impossible. Just before coming to court, I received a copy of this urgent application for provisional release, and although we will be responding in writing tomorrow, I would like to raise a few points. I am concerned that the application raises the spectre that Mr. Stanisic's life is presently in imminent jeopardy. It states in paragraph 7, "One has now to face a potential life-threatening situation in that the patient will lose any will and ability to recovery at all." This is based on a reported communication with the medical staff last Friday. Paragraph 7 characterises that, "Shared with us in order to prevent further harm to the patient that the medical staff of the UNDU is very concerned about the visible declination of the patient's condition." I note at the end of just about all of Dr. Falke's reports to the registrar, he commits to informing him immediately of any sudden alteration of his condition. In his 3rd of May report he states to Mr. Hocking, "If any problem occurs, I will inform you immediately." I would inquire whether the Chamber, I mean has the Chamber heard anything from the registrar. The Prosecution was certainly not notified that Dr. Falke had notified the registrar of any sudden and imminent or urgent change in Mr. Stanisic's condition, and so I'm troubled that the characterisation or the information provided to Defence counsel last Friday seems to be at odds with what the undertaking of Dr. Falke to notify the registrar in the event of any sudden change in his condition. In paragraph 11 of the submission, the Defence submits, "That the clinical picture which has been observed throughout the preceding weeks and months shows that the physical and mental condition of the accused has seriously deteriorated during detention." This is contradicted by reports the Chamber has received which indicate modest but measurable improvement of his psychological health and with respect, with excepting for his recent and anticipated episode of pouchitis, his intestinal problems have not been a recurring problem. If we look --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request to read a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, if we look it in an objective measure of his pouchitis such as the Heidelberg scale, Dr. Cazemir rates it as an 8 out of 12. If we look back at what some of what the other experts have also rated it at an earlier point in time, we can see whether or not there has been a deterioration. Dr. Taribar [phoen], the -- Mr. Stanisic's treating doctor on the 3rd of March, rated it as 9 out of 12. So it seems there might be some improvement according to Dr. Taribar. With respect to the court-appointed gastroenterologist expert Dr. Fitter on the 25th of February, Dr. Fitter assessed it at 8 out of 12, the same as Dr. Cazemir. And Dr. Van Boomgaard, well, he uses a slightly different scale. He assessed it as 8 to 10 on the Mayo Clinic scale. Verbally he described it as moderate pouchitis which demonstrates that it's comparable. So when we look at the objective scales used by these different experts, there in fact really has been no significant deterioration in the pouchitis. The problem that he's experiencing now is one that was anticipated and predicted by the experts. I imagine there's an element of hyperbole in the Defence statement that Mr. Stanisic is now barely recognizable to them. While there has been some report that he has lost weight by some of the doctors, it's not measured in any verifiable way against earlier medical reports. I hardly believe that the Defence counsel is now having difficulty in recognising Mr. Stanisic. In paragraph 12, the Defence suggests that it is clear that the accused cannot recover while in the UN detention unit. "This view has been confirmed by the treating psychiatrist Dr. Petrovic who has indicated that all remedies have been exhausted and the only avenue which remains is for the accused to be provided with the clinical environment with treatment from a team of multi-disciplinary experts. Also in paragraph 15 of the motion, "However, they," meaning the UN detention unit medical staff, "recognise that they are unable to bring about a recovery in this environment." Compare that with the last paragraph of Dr. Falke's report a week ago on the 13th of May, "I also discussed the situation with Dr. Vera Petrovic, his treating psychiatrist, yesterday. Although she agrees that there is a significant improvement in his depression, she advises strongly against the use of the videolink at this stage due to fear of relapse." If we look at Dr. Falke's report of the 9th of May, "Should his mental state continue to show the level of the improvement seen in the past week as it is in the integration of cognitive functions that is lacking in a deep depression," he goes on to say "he should be capable of instructing counsel in the coming weeks." So the statements today and the assertions made in the application are contradicted by the most recent positive indications that we have received from the medical staff. I submit that it's curious that Dr. Petrovic's last report acknowledges significant improvement and then one week later, Dr. Petrovic is saying she's reached the plateau, there's nothing else that she can do. The application request that Mr. Stanisic be released from detention, returned to Belgrade to rehabilitate himself in an army hospital and at a spa at Igalo, Montenegro. Prior to coming to court I took a quick look at the Igalo facility and what they offer and I have copies here that I'd ask the usher to assist me with in and distributing, and it lists the medical programmes and the medical care that Igalo is able to provide its clients. I can't help imagine that the thousands of victims of crimes the Prosecution alleges Mr. Stanisic is responsible for, I can't help but imagine that those victims would be deeply shocked and offended at the idea that Mr. Stanisic was now asking the Court to allow him to attend this spa, this medical section replete with photographs of smiling people bathing in whirlpool baths, swimming in swimming pools, happily enjoying back massages and saunas. The only ailment that Mr. Stanisic has that they list as something they treat is osteoporosis. It approaches the boundaries of mockery to suggest that what Mr. Stanisic needs in order to improve his health for the rigors of trial is not the careful care of Holland's best medical practitioners but spa treatments in a vacation resort. I do intend to respond in writing to this application for provisional release. I raise these issues today because of the limited time and because of the seriousness of this -- there's such a gap between what Mr. Knoops is asserting now and what the medical evidence is. It seems to me that either Mr. Stanisic's condition has so rapidly and so severely deteriorated in the last few days, and if that is the case, it must be dealt with immediately to safeguard his well being, or the Chamber and the Prosecution have been misinformed about his health, for what Mr. Knoops reports the medical staff is saying to him is in direct opposition to the written reports they have filed, and this is an unacceptable situation that must be investigated and resolved immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I notice Mr. Groome that the Igalo facility has 51 physicians. Why would they ever 51 physicians if they were just a kind of a tourist resort?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure. I'm still in the process of investigating this. It says they have 51 physicians and 93 registered nurses, but if you look at the ailments that they treat, the openly one, as I say is, osteoporosis. That is certainly being treated by Mr. Stanisic's primary care providers now. It would seem to me if the allegation or the assertion is that Mr. Stanisic is no longer fit for the detention unit, that one, it must be -- should be evaluated by the Pieter Baan Centre which is equipped to do that and secondly, the Pieter Baan Centre is a full medical facility. It has every capability to deal with any ailment that Mr. Stanisic has, so perhaps during his time, if the Court were to consider that or send him to Pieter Baan Centre, they would be able to deal with his health problems in a comprehensive manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops will no doubt wish to comment on this brochure and say whether it's a fair representation of the work done by that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for giving the Defence this opportunity. If the Court allows me, I will not go into all the details because I believe this is something for the proceedings on the motion. But, Your Honour, we are not acting here to ensure that Mr. Stanisic will receive a treatment in some kind of a spa. We are here because we believe, with us the detention unit at this moment, that he deserves to receive the proper medical treatment. And indeed, the reports of the UNDU always have stressed that despite some slight changes in his mood in a positive way, there was always a fear of relapse, so I think it's not fair to pinpoint the physicians who are treating Mr. Stanisic to their earlier reports if they at the same time stressed that fear of relapse exists, and this is exactly what the Court can envision by the last report of Dr. Falke, the last paragraph which is in my humble submission not a matter of hearsay. Dr. Falke relies on an existing report of Dr. Petrovic which he uses and cites in his last report of today which exactly evidences this relapse. At the same time, that being said, it shows the deterioration in his current form, namely that the detention centre has exhausted the possibilities for treatment of this person and therefore, we don't believe that the motion as it's lying before the Court is exaggerating the situation. Your Honour, before addressing some of the remarks of Mr. Groome and also your question as to the institution of Igalo, I would like to remind the Prosecution to the fact that the Appeals Chamber, in its ruling of last Friday, refers to a period of a minimum of three months. The Prosecution is already quite premature in addressing the Court with suggestions that Mr. Stanisic can be medically well prepared in three months and that the Pieter Baan Centrum is able to assess the situation over three months, but the Appeals Chamber has put it quite clearly that we're dealing with a situation which take -- or could take at a minimum three months. And the Chamber also, when reading legally, refers to the term "before determining when the trial should commence." Now, my learned friend of the Prosecution, Mr. Groome, used the words, "When the trial should continue." I believe there is a legal distinction between continuation of a trial and a commencement of the trial and therefore, I believe that the Appeals Chamber has clearly in mind that before this trial should again commence, the Court should reassess indeed the situation. It's not fair to say that the Appeals Chamber did not elucidate on the fitness of the situation because the fitness issue as such was not part of the appeal, as Your Honours know. Secondly, I think that the comparison with the Milosevic situation and the report of Judge Parker is misplaced. In all due respect, it's misplaced simply because there is no evidence before this Court that Mr. Stanisic was able to manipulate for the period of three months the whole medical staff at the UNDU, Dr. Cazemir, and all the treating experts in this regard. This is not clearly any indication to that. And otherwise, it would have been reported to the Chamber. And how, and it's my personal remark, Your Honour, this person who is at the edge of his physical and mental abilities, was sinking down to the minimum of surviving would flush down medication into the toilet to put his life further at danger, I think it's not a realistic picture of we, as Defence, have experienced throughout the last months, with us the medical staff and the experts. Now, as to the depression, indeed, Dr. Petrovic indicated in her earlier report that there was an improvement but at the same time, she warned the parties that there could be a real fear for relapse. And I believe what Your Honours have before it is the last report of Dr. Falke in which report it is stated that Dr. Petrovic has received a plateau in her ability to treat Mr. Stanisic without the assistance of a multi-disciplinary team in a medical environment. We're not asking for a release of Mr. Stanisic. We are asking for a release to put him in a medical environment. That's the distinction. The Prosecution is sketching the picture as though the crimes for which Mr. Stanisic is charged would not anticipate such a situation, but I think this is not the criterion we should measure the case about. Now, two remarks as to the Pieter Baan Centrum and to Igalo. The booklet we just were provided with is familiar with the Defence. I know the articles that are written by some of the members of the Pieter Baan Centrum, but what the Prosecution is not telling the Court is that the Pieter Baan Centrum is a testing institution. It's not a treating institution. It does not treat patients who are seriously ill akin to Mr. Stanisic. That institution, in our law, is there to provide the Court within 6 or 9 months or on the basis of an observation of 6 until 9 weeks a report on the mental state to indeed participate in proceedings. It does not assess the fitness for provisional release. It can only assess the fitness for detention after a potential conviction. We're dealing here with a situation of provisional release. Now, for that purpose, in due respect, we don't think that the Pieter Baan Centrum could assist the Court in providing information other than the Court has in its possession about the eligibility of the accused for provisional release. I agree with my learned friend from the Prosecution that of course some kind of objective supervision, as I already informed the Court of, is in place, but that can more practically be done by either Dr. Petrovic and the Prosecution acknowledges that she travels regularly back and forth from The Hague to Serbia, can be done by Dr. Cazemir to "could go to any institution on a regular basis or Dr. de Man." As to the Pieter Baan Centrum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Looking at the brochure, they might not mind going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said looking at the brochure, the doctors might not mind travelling to the Igalo Centre. It appears to have its own attractions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That is possible, yes, Your Honour. I will come back to the Igalo option in a second. Your Honour, maybe that the Court can recall that Dr. de Man, when we questioned him about the Pieter Baan Centrum, it was the Defence who asked Dr. de Man about the Pieter Baan concurred with the Defence, agreeing with the Defence saying indeed, the Pieter Baan Centrum is not there to treat with a multi-disciplinary team over three months such a patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So are you able to tell us, Mr. Knoops, generally for how long do patients stay at the centre, the Pieter Baan Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Six to nine weeks for observation, then the team of the Pieter Baan Centrum submits a report to the court. We have a provision in our law which goes to mental disease so it's actually a reporting institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say that it's not a treating centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, it's not a treating centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in the six to nine weeks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- what are they doing, only testing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No treating?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Interviews by several experts of the accused, the psychiatrists, psychologists, social worker and other experts in order to write a report to the Court as to the mental capabilities of an accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But while they are there, who would be responsible for the treatment of the particular individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It's based on a court order, such a referral of such a accused to the Pieter Baan Centrum. The Pieter Baan Centrum itself works under the supervision of the Ministry of Justice in the Netherlands but in our system we need a court order to have an accused admitted to the Pieter Baan Centrum, of course, the Dutch court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand. How can a patient be at a medical institution for six to nine weeks, the patient has a particular medical condition. Now that patient is only being tested, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I'm asking what about the treatment? Is that treatment being provided by some other institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No. After the Pieter Baan Centrum has reported, filed a report with the Court as to the mental capacities of an accused to understand the charges or as to the fact of diminished responsibility, which is in our law, a matter of potential mitigation of sentence, the Court will address the case again and when the Pieter Baan Centrum would advise a medical treatment, the mental treatment of the accused, the Court has to decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, it's just the logical situation that defeats me because if in the six to nine weeks that patient is not being treated, is only being tested --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- isn't there a likelihood that his medical condition will deteriorate? It seems to me that he must be getting some treatment. It can't be just testing. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe I can be of assistance. I put these specific questions to the director of the Pieter Baan Centre last Friday. With respect to the physical ailments, we actually put to him the actual complaints and the condition of Mr. Stanisic, and he said that they would be able to get him whatever treatment he needs, that -- and if there's any outside specialists needed, they can be brought in or if he has to be -- if he has some kind of urgent event that he has to be brought to a hospital that can be done. With respect to the period of time, he says under Dutch law, it's a maximum of seven weeks so it's a five to seven-week observation period that they typically have someone there. I put it to Mr. Heidelberg the director what about his psychological state, is there a responsibility possibility that that could deteriorate, are you able to manage that? He said yes, they can manage that as well. They will do whatever has to be done with respect to his treatment for his psychological state to ensure that there's no deterioration of that. So he will be treated on a psychological basis and a medical basis, plus he will be evaluated for a period of five to seven weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exactly -- this is exactly what I mean. Five to seven weeks, this institution is primarily there for testing. Of course it can provide medical assistance in order for an accused to medically survive those five until seven weeks, of course. There is no doubt that a gastroenterologist can be brought in, but the primary function of this institution is an observation testing period of five to seven weeks and I think we all agree that what Mr. Stanisic needs is more than five to seven weeks. Therefore, that institution could be at the utmost come into play when the Court would wish to reassess the medical situation of Mr. Stanisic after full medical treatment by a multi-disciplinary team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, my brother has just shown me that under the heading "care" during detention, they have "improving the disorder through treatment," so they do provide treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: They do provide treatment, Your Honour, but this is not their -- the institution is not primarily aiming at a treatment we have in mind with this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to counter that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to be assured that treatment would be provided as well as testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, the Prosecution disputes that although it is not directly inclining manipulation by the accused, it is disputing that a person could deteriorate in such a short period but if I may just briefly take the attention of the Court to the reports we indeed received last Friday by Dr. Cazemir, a loss of weight of 12 kilogrammes, 20 stools or more a day, severe loss of blood, et cetera, when we notice that in three months, Mr. Stanisic suffered twice a kidney attack, because this is also new in the report last Sunday night, he had again a severe kidney attack. It's it is the second time while in detention during the last three months. It cannot be ignored that this can be faked or this is not any exponent of deterioration. The medication as being tried by Dr. Cazemir has been changed and changed without any results and all those data are verifiable to the Court including the new report of Dr. Petrovic. As to Igalo, finally, Your Honour. Igalo also has of course also a clinical department. Your Honour can recall that the accused spent in the past several times in Igalo and the argument of the Prosecution that it's more a vacation centre was put earlier before the Chamber. I would not again asserting that Mr. Stanisic should go to this environment. What we are aiming at is primarily a hospitalisation preferably in his own environment in Belgrade in the Military Medical Academy where all the disciplines we need to have him recovered are in place. And we know from the past that the reporting system is quite efficient and effective. Secondly, yes, Your Honours may observe from the request the suggestion for a potential additional treatment in Igalo was not put as a primary option. It's simply an option the Court can have in mind, and the reason why we put it already in this motion is to prevent the costly and time-consuming proceedings we went through in the past when, for instance, one of the treating doctors in the Military Medical Hospital would advise a short additional treatment for a specific problem Mr. Stanisic suffered from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an option you would not want us to consider the Pieter Baan Centre, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Our primary option is the Military Medical Hospital, Your Honour, and if Your Honours would think it is practical to also deal with the option that on the advice of one of the treating specialists, an Igalo referral is tenable, then of course we would not oppose that, of course, we would act against the interest of the accused if the doctor would so suggest. But maybe there is no advice from any of those physicians in Belgrade and therefore, Mr. Stanisic would never arrive at this centre. Lastly, I forgot to mention when we speak about the argument of the Prosecution, the suggestion of potential manipulation, I would say, and I would submit that the Prosecution is selectively quoting from the evidence. Your Honour know that from the reports we receive from the government, the reports the Prosecution selects from, namely the day he went to various locations, Your Honour may remember that the Defence addressed that argument by explaining every moment what Mr. Stanisic did and that those activities did not require any physical intensity. Secondly, a few days later there was an observation whereby Mr. Stanisic -- was the whole day in his own environment at home so also here, there is no -- we cannot conclude anything from that observation. In sum, we believe although the Prosecution will address tomorrow the arguments in writing, we believe that the Court has the possibilities on the basis of the existing evidence to consider this motion. We don't believe that additional evidence is necessary for the Chamber to come to that conclusion. As to the Pieter Baan Centrum, we believe it's premature now to set up an evaluation system for after just three months the Prosecution mentions, in our view a minimum of three months because nobody knows where the mental health will go from now. We believe that the information we received from the staff of the detention centre still fits within the statement Dr. Falke gave to the Court today. If there is any doubt, I have no problem that the Court verifies that stance, but we were alarmed by the situation on Friday, evidenced Sunday night by this severe attack and therefore, we believe it is our responsibility as Defence to bring this matter as soon as possible to the Court. Dr. Falke reported to the registry and therefore, I think he fulfilled his duty by bringing this matter to the registry because he writes, this is the last sentence of his report, "I regard this opinion as important," referring to the opinion of Dr. Petrovic. Therefore, it fully complies with the existing reporting system and there is no suspicion whatsoever to be issued by the Prosecution as to the severity of the medical situation at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you sit, may I just remind the court deputy that earlier, I had required that the opinion of Dr. Petrovic to which reference is made by Dr. Falke in the last paragraph of his report be submitted to the Chamber as quickly as possible. We would like to have that preferably by the end of the day. Now, I wanted to ask you, Mr. Knoops, whether your application for provisional release is wholly exclusively linked, tied, to the medical condition of the accused. Under Rule 65, "Provisional release is only to be granted if the Chamber is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person." Are you tying your application wholly to the medical condition or are you saying that you can satisfy us, because as you know, the burden is on you, it's discharged on a balance of probabilities, you can satisfy us as to these matters and the health condition is an additional factor that can be advanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this question. I think it self-evident that the application refers specifically and relies specifically upon Rule 65. The indeed primary basis of it is the medical condition, this is our concern. I already stressed we are not here to seek a release in the grammatic sense of the word. We are seeking provisional release in order to have Mr. Stanisic being transferred to preferably the Military Medical Hospital. Now, as to the conditions of Rule 65, it may be semantic but we can say the foundation of our request is the medical situation intertwined with the two conditions as set forth by Rule 65 or it's based on Rule of 65, i.e., its two conditions and the goal of that application is to have and receive medical treatment. I still believe that in both scenarios, Rule 65 is the proper foundation for the request. As to the concern of the Chamber with respect to compliance of the accused to those conditions, I respectfully refer to the past that Mr. Stanisic, in our view, has always complied with the conditions and has returned to the Court despite his illness. I don't believe, although I'm not an expert, I don't believe that a person who is that ill is capable or even willing to think of endangering his process and, as Rule 65 sets out, will pose a danger to any victim, witness, or any person. I cannot believe that on the basis of the evidence before the Chamber, a person who has sunken down to the minimum of living is able to think of that interest, if an interest at all. I'm not testifying from the bar, Your Honour, and from the table, but I would like to stress that the way we have now perceived the situation during the last few weeks also in our view deteriorated such that in a way, physically, the defendant is recognizable for us, but not any more as an intellectual human being to whom one can on a sensible way communicate with. I cannot believe that such a human being is capable of misusing such a situation instead of surviving, recovering from a grave situation, which also is out of the control -- and I'm not blaming anyone, but we simply observe that the medical situation is out of control of the people who are now treating him. Dr. Petrovic clearly says, and we knew on Friday this observation already, that she has reached her maximum to do what she can within her best abilities to make this person better. And in this view, in this context, it's hardly imaginable that Mr. Stanisic would pose a danger for the Court, the integrity of the Court, the proceedings and the victims and witnesses. It's up to the Court to decide, of course, but I would like to stress that this is our sincere belief and it's not our belief that the accused is here to misuse the situation and we sincerely hope that the Court will not accept the Prosecution's insinuation that a form of manipulation is present either in taking medication or misusing the situation the Appeals Chamber now has set forth, namely an adjournment for at a minimum of three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give me your view on this: The trial started, the accused was on bail, on provisional release prior to the trial. The trial started, and we now have the Appeals Chamber's ruling. Does the fact that the trial had started mean anything in a consideration of provisional release? Normally, accused persons who are on bail and then brought to trial are not usually granted provisional release or bail, the term used in the common law, during trial and the reason, I would think, would be that the trial is on and the possibility of an outcome that is unfavourable to the accused is so much more imminent. But I don't believe that there is anything in principle that would prohibit a Trial Chamber from granting bail to an accused during a trial. I'm leaving aside for the moment the issue as to whether one would say we are in a trial at this stage, in light of the Appeals Chamber's ruling, and I understand and I will be reading very shortly some -- there are some decisions of the Appeals Chamber itself that deal with this issue. But I'd like you to address that and also Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this question. In the first place, Your Honour, I believe legally, this case is back in pre-trial. When reading the Appeals Chamber decision of the 16th of May closely, especially the disposition of the Chamber, it specifically, and I already alluded to that, refers to the words "the trial should commence" instead of "the trial should continue." Legally that means that this trial should commence again, with again an opening statement and the first witness and as a consequence, in our humble submission, the case is now back in pre-trial. As a result, Rule 65, in its full scope is applicable. In the alternative, I still believe that there are cases before the ICTY whereby pending trial, accused persons were released on bail or with other conditions and as such, Rule 65 does not prevent an extension to those situations. Therefore, I don't believe that the Court is prevented from using article -- sorry, Rule 65 for such -- to deal with such request. In the alternative, of course, we have relied also on the human rights provision in Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Now we are not suggesting any that Mr. Stanisic's treatment here at the UNDU is a form of degrading or inhumane treatment. What we are saying is as a result of his overall condition, he is suffering himself a situation akin to Article 3 and the view the European Court has set forth of the interpretation of Article 3, for instance in the case of Lorse versus the Netherlands whereby the European Court has assessed the applicability of Article 3 of the convention. In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, were you to succeed in this motion, it would not be on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Because that was my alternative argument. I'm not saying that Article 3 as such could be the basis but the Court has -- can find -- found its foundation for a release pending a trial if the Court would say: We are still in a trial stage and not a pre-trial stage, the Court can rely on international human rights instruments and other international instruments to allow an accused person to go away from the seat of the court for any purposes such as medical treatment and I don't believe that only the Rules of Procedure and Evidence should be the basis for that. I think it's a matter of the Court's discretion to deal with such an application. But my primary argument is that there is a legal foundation in Rule 65 simply because, firstly, we are legally in a pre-trial stage, secondly, Rule 65 or the analogy thereof is also applicable in the trial stage as evidenced by various decisions of other Chambers of this Honourable Court which dealt with releases of accused persons pending trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Groome. Mr. Jovanovic, I was going to ask whether you had any application to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of the accused Simatovic wishes to present its standpoint and motion at this point so that my learned friend from the Prosecution can respond to this and it has to do with the issue of provisional release of the accused. The Defence of the accused Stanisic submitted a motion based on the deterioration in Mr. Stanisic's health and the Defence of the accused Simatovic wished to wait for the result of today's session; however, in view of this Chamber's standpoint in connection with the Appeal Chamber's decision, that is, that the trial will recommence after at least three months, the Defence of the accused Franko Simatovic believes that the grounds for the accused's Simatovic's remaining in detention throughout this period have ceased to exist especially in view of the fact that the length of this period seems uncertain. By its decision of the 6th of February of this year, the Chamber brought the accused back to the detention unit for one reason only, and that is the speedy commencement of the trial. This was the same decision in which a Pre-Trial Conference was scheduled for February and it was then twice postponed until the 18th of March ultimately, so the reason for which the accused was brought back to the detention unit no longer holds good. For this reason, the Defence feels that the Chamber could revoke its decision of the 6th of February and based on its previous decision on provisional release, the accused could be immediately released provisionally. The reasons established by the Trial Chamber in its previous decision on provisional release are still the same. The accused Franko Simatovic never tried to influence witnesses, he passed the test, so to say, envisaged in Rule 65 which is that he turned up for trial. Not only did he turn up but his Defence actively participated in implementing all the formalities needed to implement the Chamber's order. The decision received on the 6th of February in the afternoon and the accused was to be in the detention unit by the 11th. As soon as it received this decision, the Defence contacted the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Serbia which had not been informed of the decision and sought to expedite matters so that the accused could be issued with travel documents, a ticket, and so on and Franko Simatovic arrived for his trial on time. Of course he was fully aware of all the possible consequences and the possible outcome of the trial and he complied with the Trial Chamber's order. Of course he will do the same again. The guarantees put forward in these proceedings in relation to the accused Franko Simatovic, when he first applied for provisional release and when this was granted him, are still valid. Let me remind the Chamber that every government in the Republic of Serbia is duty-bound to issue such guarantees based on the law on the cooperation between the Republic of Serbia and the ICTY and consequently of course, it respects these guarantees. The Defence can immediately submit a written motion for provisional release but let me repeat, all the facts and all the reasons established previously remain unaltered. The same reasons hold good. So if I may present my motion in this way, let me do it now. Otherwise I will submit my written motion tomorrow. Let me remind the Chamber that the trial has practically already started and whether an accused may be granted provisional release in the course of a trial, the practice in the Milan Milutinovic et al. case shows that only five days after commencement of trial, the accused were released on provisional release. Under Rule 98 bis, this may granted in the course of the trial, so if this Chamber wishes to keep this -- these proceedings as a trial, not a pre-trial, it may still grant provisional release. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not require you to submit a written, motion, Mr. Jovanovic. We consider that the presentation that you have made is sufficient for the purposes of Rule 65. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would state for the record that the Prosecution would -- does want to make a written submission with respect to both, so if the Court is willing to accept an oral application on such an important matter then it's within the discretion of the Court but the Prosecution would insist on having the opportunity to fully inform the Court of its position in writing, and I did not come here today prepared to make final arguments on such an important matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We had said by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just with respect to that, obviously it's very important the Prosecution have that report of Dr. Petrovic so I would ask that if the registrar could be instructed to give that to us promptly and if for some reason it comes late in the day, we will still endeavour to get our filing done tomorrow but obviously that's such an important piece of evidence that we would want an opportunity to express our views about it. Your Honour, with respect -- the first thing I'd like to address is respect to this issue of whether we are on trial or not. It's my understanding that the Appeals Chamber has not granted a mistrial in this case. Now, while Mr. -- to read into their use of the word "commence" as opposed to "recommence" that they've voided all proceedings so far and they've granted a mistrial to raise the possibility of a double jeopardy claim by the accused, to do that implicitly just defies common sense. I think the plain reading of the Appeals Chamber decision is that we are on trial and they have mandated a minimum or a three-month adjournment and required the Trial Chamber to assess the health of the accused. If for some reason the Chamber is in doubt about that, it seems to me the proper course of action is for us to seek clarification from the Appeals Chamber but I cannot accept that we -- that the Appeals Chamber has implicitly nullified the opening statement and initial evidence tendered by the Prosecution. With respect to the standard of whether -- the standard for provisional release changes after a trial is commenced, it does. I admit that I am conversant, I did not come to court prepared to discuss that area of the jurisprudence other than it's always a higher standard. Usually it's granted on humanitarian grounds, but I would like to deal with that fully in writing rather than be talking without being able to cite the specific jurisprudence. There is ample jurisprudence now in this area. With respect to the Court's consideration of a provisional release in this case, I mean it must be the result of a full and careful consideration by the Chamber. Respectfully, Mr. Jovanovic is very wrong when he says that nothing has changed. On the 11th of May there was an election in Serbia and there is still no government formed. They are unable to form a government. The Court must explore the reliability and the -- of the guarantees that would be proffered. One of the parties that had a significant showing in the -- in that election was the SPS party. Its leader Mr. Nikolic has said publicly on numerous, numerous occasions that if the SPS comes into power, all cooperation with this Tribunal will cease and he is explicitly made an appeal to indictees saying to that them if I am elected you will not be sent to The Hague. So to say that there is no change of circumstances is just utterly wrong. If the Chamber is going to consider granting this remedy, it is the Prosecution's position that it can only be after a full and careful consideration with -- and that the Chamber should wait until a government is formed, a government that will last a period of time, the period of time for this three to six months or whatever this adjournment will ultimately end up being and that the Chamber wait until representatives of that newly-formed government can appear before it and give the guarantees that satisfy the Chamber need to have both accused return and proceed with the trial. With respect to Mr. Knoops, it seems that he's not asking for Mr. Stanisic to be placed at liberty but simply that his place of treatment be altered. He seems to be suggesting that he's quite content that Mr. Stanisic be placed in the -- there is a secure ward of the military hospital, that perhaps he's suggesting that he is seeking that. It would be helpful to have a clarification of that before we draft our motion because I think that alters our response to it. Then the question becomes where is the most appropriate place for him to be treated. Your Honour, there is one other matter I would like to raise with the Court I would ask that we go into private session briefly just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to just correct. I misspoke. It's the SRS party not the SPS party so it's the SRS party that has made these very public claims that cooperation with the Tribunal will cease. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And they are part of the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours we are in open session at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And this party is what, is likely to form a government?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was an election a few weeks ago, May 11th and the results were inconclusive. There was different numbers of parliamentary seats won by the various parties. They are now struggling to try to form a coalition government. They have not been successful so far, but the SRS party was one of the parties that had a significant showing and its leaders have been publicly stating that it would cease cooperation with the Tribunal if it were in a position to do so, that it had control of the government, and that's something that the Chamber I believe has to be very mindful of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to remind you of this: In reviewing the case, the motion for provisional release, the Prosecution had the same arguments. At that time, they stated that the government of the Republic of Serbia, regardless of which parties were forming the government then, that they would not honour the guarantees and that they would not extradite the accused, and this Trial Chamber and also the Appeals Chamber assessed that the position and conduct of the accused towards this Tribunal was relevant when they made their decision and this conduct was such that Franko Simatovic, the accused, on his first appearance stated that he considers this Trial Chamber or this court to be a domestic court, a court of his own country and that he considered it incumbent upon him to appear before this Court. I also don't think that it is appropriate to analyse the political situation in Serbia when considering this. What the Prosecution is stating that a member of the Serbian Radical Party publicly said, Mr. Tomislav Nikolic, about this cooperation with the Tribunal was actually during the preelection campaign and I also want to remind you that the leader of that party voluntarily surrendered to this Court. Also I would like to remind you that there is a legal obligation, there is a law on cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal and issuance of guarantees that are to be observed are issued based on this law so if anyone should want to neglect this law, they would have to change the law in the regular procedure. For the time being, the Serbian Radical Party does not have this option to form a government on its own. They are currently negotiating with the Serbian Democratic Party as a possible coalition party, and let me remind you that President Kostunica is the leader of that party and it is precisely during his Presidency that the largest number of accused actually surrendered to the ICTY. At this point it is not clear who will be able to form the government and what kind of coalition will be built, but as I mentioned already, this is a legal obligation and it is not up to any political party to follow these -- this law on its own. And I am certain that any future government will cooperate with this Tribunal and whatever individuals may state during a campaign, I have to remind you that this is just something that's said in a campaign. Now, the accused Ojdanic was released provisionally. He returned on the 11th of May in other words, one day after the elections, so the fact that the government was dismissed and that there were new elections had no effect on this decision of the Trial Chambers in the case of Milutinovic and others so I think this is something to be considered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please clarify exactly what it is that you are requesting. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- our request is a provisional release in order to have Mr. Stanisic treated in a non-custodial, secure environment which primarily, in our view, is the Military Medical Hospital but if the treatment dictates so, and the treating doctors would advise so, including the doctors who would advise the Court or report to the Court, the Defence asked the Court not to exclude a further treatment in a private environment, i.e., at and within the private chambers of the accused, but our primary goal is to have him treated in a non-custodial secure environment. The Military Medical Hospital is secure, it's a secure building, it's totally secure, because nobody can get in or out without permission of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you unnecessarily restricting yourself? If he is entitled provisional release, can you satisfy us as to the conditions in Rule 65?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not necessarily in a -- in a particular hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this regard, I'm maybe too modest in my expression and I would not necessarily restrict the request to the treatment in a non-custodial and secure environment. We do want to leave the option open that Mr. Stanisic, if the treatment has been successful in the Military Medical Hospital and further, adaptation in society is necessary for his full recovery, we would not exclude the possibility that Mr. Stanisic could further recover in his private environment. In this way, I think that the Prosecution is entitled to respond to the request as we have put it in the motion, not only restricted to purely a non-custodial and secure environment but that it should be understood as including any form of treatment which is dictated by the experts and the findings. But of course to have a start for such recovery, we believe that it should start in a medical institution such as the Military Medical Hospital but we would not like to necessarily restrict us to that institution or exclude any other possibilities for recovery in society. Now, Your Honour, if I just have my last remark on my learned friend's comments on whether or not a clarification is necessitated by the Appeals Chamber as to the reading of the decision of the 16th of May, the Court will have noticed that the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 3 of its decision acknowledges that the Appeals Chamber notes that the trial in this case commenced on the 28th April 2008, yet the -- in which decision is from the 9th April 2008. Now I agree with my learned friend that the Appeals Chamber did not conclude that a mistrial has been conducted because I don't believe this is actually the stage where the Appeals Chamber has authority to say so. But it's from the deposition clear that the Appeals Chamber reverses the impugned decision of the 9th of April that is several weeks before the commencement of the trial on the 28th of April 2008, i.e., the opening statement. So from the deposition, it's clear and therefore that's totally understandable why the Chamber, Appeals Chamber specifically uses the word "commence" that by reversing that decision of the 9th of April, the Appeals Chamber implicitly conveys the message that because that decision is reversed, it was way before the opening statement, the start of the case, the trial technically, that therefore, the trial should commence again. This is I think the way we should read the Appeals Chamber's decision and I don't see a reason why the parties should seek clarification from the Appeals Chamber. It would take additional time for this urgent matter and although I understand the argument my learned friend just put in closed session, I would respectfully ask the Court to deal with the request without having a specific hearing. I believe we have the hearing and we are grateful for Your Honours' time that we could address the Court today on this matter but if the Court, on request of the Prosecution, would now schedule a hearing for next week on this issue, in our humble submission, it's probably difficult to have this delay in terms of the resolution of the medical situation of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber was considering initially having a hearing but I would think that we have had a very full discussion today and the Chamber, I believe, has profited from the arguments that have been submitted. It's something that I, of course, would discuss with my colleagues again, but I very much doubt that it will be necessary to schedule another hearing. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just briefly, in the Seselj case, that was a case in which the Appeals Chamber did order a restart to the trial. In its decision of the 8th of December, 2006 it used -- explicitly stated, "The trial is suspended." I mean, it was very clear. It didn't implicitly cause the trial to be restarted. It was very explicit in its determination that the trial had to be restarted. With respect to hearing, I know the Chamber's heard ample arguments today but I submit that what is essential and what we are hearing would be useful and required is to have a representative of the government come and to discuss with the Chamber the reliability or their ability to commit the next government that is yet to be formed to a guarantee that they would produce Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic if necessary. These were not the same arguments that were put to the Chamber or to the representative at the initial provisional release hearing. The argument that was put at that stage was that, failing to have produced General Mladic, someone who there was good information was in Serbia, whether that guarantee could be relied upon, and the Chamber sought fit to rely on it. There is a very different situation where there is a government yet to be formed and the Chamber would be seeking to rely on a guarantee given by a government that is in its final days in office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jovanovic, and I believe you will be the last to make a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. The legal deadline for forming a government in Serbia is in September, so if we wait to hear a representative of the new government, we might have to wait until such time as this trial is due to restart. All the arguments have already been put forward. The Trial Chamber has already ruled based on these reasons. The fact that Radovan Karadzic, Ratko Mladic, Zupljanin and others are still at large was put forward as an argument against provisional release when the original decision was made, but it was precisely when a government was in power that the Prosecution was expressing misgivings about, 20 accused arrived at this Tribunal. The Law on Cooperation between the Republic of Serbia and the ICTY will not be amended. The Prosecutor has not put forward any reasons that might lead us to reconsider. They have not put forward any new arguments. The prime minister and deputy prime minister are continuing to carry out their essential tasks until the new government is formed and that might be in September, as I said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We thank you all for the submissions that you have made. The Chamber will give a decision on the provisional release application as quickly as possible, recognising its importance, and we hope to do so by Friday of this week. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.56 p.m.
